catalyst.action: Accumulate in thirds across the 14.40-15.30 zone; add a further third only under 13.50 if it gets there. No need to hurry and no reason to chase above 15.30. Hold for a multiple re-rating over roughly six to eight quarters, not for a print.

thesis: Conagra earned $1.72 over the last four reported quarters (0.41, 0.47, 0.39, 0.45 from the fetched surprise record) and closed at 15.29, which is 8.9 times trailing earnings for a branded packaged-food company with a dividend. That is a multiple normally paid for a business in decline, and the results do not show one: CAG beat consensus in three of the last four quarters, including by 43.9% in the September quarter. The sell side has effectively given up — of 25 analysts, zero rate it strong buy, one buy, 14 hold, eight sell and two strong sell, a 4.0% bullish share, which is among the most negative distributions I have seen on a company of this size. Against that unanimity, an insider bought 35,000 shares at 14.5895 on 2026-07-17, about $510,632, with no insider sales in six months. The target of 20.50 is 12 times the $1.72 already earned — below where packaged food has historically traded and requiring no earnings growth at all, only that the multiple stop pricing an imminent collapse.
key_risk: This is a value trap until proven otherwise, and the ten analysts with sell ratings are not being stupid. The structural bear case on packaged food is real: GLP-1 adoption reducing calorie consumption, private label taking share in centre-of-store categories, and grocers pressing margin on branded suppliers. Any of those can grind earnings down for years while the multiple stays at 9x, which is how a cheap stock stays cheap and why a stock at 8.9x is not automatically a bargain. The invalidation is concrete rather than a price move: a dividend cut, or trailing-twelve-month EPS falling below $1.45 for two consecutive quarters, means volume decline is beating cost control and the thesis is wrong — exit regardless of price. Note also that at a $197M average daily dollar volume this is a mid-cap in liquidity terms, not a mega-cap.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is the one the sell side is making: at 8.9x the market is not mispricing Conagra, it is correctly discounting secular volume decline, and buying it is buying a melting ice cube with a dividend. The answer has to be in the earnings rather than in the multiple, and it is — a business losing a secular war does not beat consensus in three of four quarters or print a 43.9% upside surprise in its most recent one, which is what the fetched record shows. The second leg of the answer is the insider: a 35,000-share open-market purchase with zero offsetting sales is someone with the volume data choosing to buy at 14.59, which is a different kind of evidence from a multiple argument. Where I concede the point is in the structure of the trade — hence a six-to-eight-quarter horizon, an accumulation plan rather than a position, and an invalidation written on EPS and the dividend rather than on the share price, because if the bears are right the tell will show up in earnings long before any stop would help.

catalyst.event: October CPI at 08:30 ET on 2026-11-10 (consensus headline +0.2% MoM, core +0.3% MoM), then NVDA earnings 2026-11-17 amc as the test of whether the AI leg keeps losing sponsorship
catalyst.action: WAIT FOR THE CPI PRINT — do not front-run it. After 08:30 ET, work the 277.00-279.50 zone only if core came in at or below the +0.3% consensus. A hot core print lifts the 10-year from an already-high 4.86% and small caps are the most rate-sensitive of the three index ETFs, so an upside surprise invalidates the entry timing rather than improving the discount. Do not pay 282.51 after a 3.2% session. Take the first target at 298.50 into the 11-17 NVDA print rather than holding for 305.

thesis: Small caps are the only major US index ETF to have repaired its trend, and the outperformance was earned during the drawdown rather than in a bounce. Over the last month IWM returned +1.28% while SPY fell 3.32% and QQQ fell more still — IWM beat SPY by 4.60 points and QQQ by 10.85 points, in the same month the Nasdaq fell into a 3.4% weekly decline and a $2.5T AI de-rating. If this were small-cap beta it would have fallen harder, which is exactly what it did over 3m (-3.82 vs SPY) and 6m (-2.80). It did the opposite, so money is moving by mandate rather than by risk appetite. The structure confirms it: IWM closed 282.51, above its 20-day (277.07), 50-day (281.84) and 200-day (279.09), while SPY (752.69) and QQQ (679.35) both remain below their 20- and 50-day, QQQ by 5.7% and 11% off its high. Entry is the 277.00-279.50 shelf where the 20-day and 200-day converge.
key_risk: A rotation out of 40% of the index market cap is not usually a bullish event for the other 60% — if the AI de-rating turns into broad de-risking, small caps have the weaker balance sheets and fall further, and Morgan Stanley’s own downside range of 7100-7300 on the S&P sits 3-6% below Monday’s close. The specific near-term risk is this morning: October CPI prints at 08:30 ET, and with the 10-year already at 4.86% a hot core number hits small caps hardest because they carry more floating-rate debt than large caps. That is the one macro input actively working against this trade and it resolves within hours, which is why the entry waits for it. A failure through 268.80 breaks the 90-day low and the reclaimed-trend premise with it.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that this is simply the fourth week of an AI unwind and IWM is up because it is the funding destination of a temporary de-grossing, not a new leadership regime — one NVDA beat on 11-17 and the money goes straight back. The 6-month relative number is the answer that makes me take the trade anyway: IWM is now ahead of QQQ by 3.77 points over six months, so this is no longer a one-month artifact of a single drawdown. But it is only a partial answer, which is why the position is sized standard rather than high conviction, the entry is a pullback rather than a market order, and the plan explicitly takes profit at the first target into the NVDA print instead of holding for the 90-day high.

catalyst.event: Chemicals at a cyclical earnings trough with the CEO buying and sell-side revisions turning up — no dated event, the catalyst is the cycle
catalyst.action: Work the 8.90-9.15 zone on a pullback into the 20-day/50-day convergence. Do not pay 9.54. There is no print to trade around — Q3 already reported — so there is no hurry and no reason to chase.

thesis: On 2026-08-03 Peter R Huntsman bought 100,000 shares at 9.81 on the open market, about $981,000, with no insider sales at the company in six months — and the stock closed 2026-11-09 at 9.54, so the entry is available below what the chief executive whose name is on the building paid for it. The second leg is the sell side turning: bullish share is 33.3% but the change is +23.8 points over four months, the largest improvement in any name I screened today, with revision direction reported as improving. Huntsman is 28.75% off its 90-day high of 13.39 in the trough of a chemicals cycle, and the entry at 8.90-9.15 is the convergence of the 20-day (9.00) and 50-day (9.01). Market cap is roughly $1.65B and average daily dollar volume $29.6M, so a 1.5% position is a small fraction of a day's trade.
key_risk: The company is losing money. Trailing twelve-month EPS is negative $0.53 (0.04, 0.00, -0.20, -0.37) and it has beaten consensus in only one of the last four quarters, missing by 42.9% and 100% in the two most recent. That means there is no valuation anchor under this position — I cannot tell you what it is worth on earnings because there are no earnings, so the floor is the cycle turning rather than a multiple, and cyclical troughs routinely last longer than a swing horizon. This is also a sub-$2B cap at a 4.76% ATR: a secondary equity or converts offering to shore up the balance sheet is the most likely way this thesis dies well before the chemicals cycle resolves, and dilution would not be contained by the stop. Position is sized at 1.5% speculative for exactly these reasons.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that insider buying at a loss-making cyclical is the cheapest signal in finance — a CEO buying a million dollars of his own trough-earnings company is both expected and nearly costless to him, and the fact that the stock is now 2.8% below his August purchase is evidence he was early rather than right. That is a fair reading and I will not pretend the earnings record argues otherwise, with one miss of 100% in the June quarter. What makes it worth 1.5% anyway is that the purchase is not the only thing that moved: a 23.8-point improvement in bullish share with revisions turning up is independent of the insider and is the sell side revising the forward numbers, not the trailing ones. The position is sized as a cycle option, not a conviction holding, and the conviction is published as 3 rather than the 4 the evidence count would support.
